title.value: RANKGUESS: Password Guessing Using Adversarial Ranking
RANKGUESS: Password Guessing Using Adversarial Ranking

abstract.value: Password security is significantly influenced by being aware of the methods potential adversaries might deploy. To this end, modeling guessing attacks has become a pivotal task. In pursuit of maximized attack efficacy, adversaries A usually attempt to guess in descending order of likelihood, akin to the way generative retrieval learning-to-rank (LTR) functions in a recommendation system, which prioritizes information to targeted users based on predicted relevance. In this paper, we propose a password guessing framework based on adversarial ranking, named RANKGUESS. We regard passwords as sequential decision trajectories. In this context, the adversaries A are assumed to train an agent where the current state is represented by the password sequence generated up to that point. The action taken is to generate the next token, and the evaluation score assigned by the ranker model serves as the reward signal received. Consequently, we frame the problem of password guessing as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and tackle using adversarial ranking techniques. Due to the generality of our approach, RANKGUESS can be applicable to further guessing scenarios (i.e., trawling password guessing, targeted password guessing based on personally identifiable information (PII), and conditional password guessing). By employing 12 large-scale password and six PII datasets, we demonstrate that our models are effective: (1) RANKGUESS surpasses all current state-of-the-art models and outperforms GAN-based methods by 26.29%∼43.69% (on average 34.80%); (2) When the victim's PII at site A (namely PIIA) is known, RANKGUESS-PII for targeted password guessing based on PIIA, which guesses 58.21%∼91.95% of common users within 10 12 guesses, outperforms foremost counterpart by 6.32%∼17.09%; (3) Within 10 7 guesses, our RANKGUESS-MASK based on victims' partial passwords (e.g., d****l*02*), enhances the password cracking success rate by approximately 7.70% to 14.85% (on average 8.21%) compared to state-ofthe-art models. Furthermore, we have meticulously analyzed the scenarios in which our model is applicable, as well as the sources of the guessing performance improvement. 1 More specifically, Pasquini et al. Introduction Passwords are the primary means of user authentica- tion [10], [92] and are crucial for the online daily activities of the approximately 5.2 billion netizens [9]. With the proliferation of online services, the number of web accounts that users need to manage constantly increases, ranging from 80 to 107 [66]. However, users typically can remember only 5 to 7 different passwords [35]. Unavoidably, users tend to choose popular strings [80], employ personally identifiable information (PII) [81], and are susceptible to side-channel attacks [63], [89] (shoulder surfing [20], keystroke audio feedback [22], etc.). Recently, internet users seem to have become accustomed to catastrophic password breaches from high-profile sites ( e.g., 3 billion Yahoo leak [2], 1.1 billion Alibaba credential breach [58]). This sudden upsurge in account usage also exposes users' passwords to a multitude of potential threats. Even with password managers, vulnera- bilities can still lead to data breaches. For example, reported allowed adversaries to access extensive customer vaults, including URLs, site credentials, and metadata [4]. Thus, it is important to understand password security in-the-wild. To this end, modeling password guessing attacks has be- come a pivotal undertaking. In practice, guess number [72] is found to be a good metric to evaluate password strength, and those easily guessed by adversaries A are considered to be weak passwords. Therefore, studying password strength from the adversaries' perspective is doubly profound. More- over, the adversaries A may gather extra information ( e.g., PII [81], or partial passwords [63]) with breached passwords to guess victims' credentials and steal property/engage in de- ception. The incessant escalation of attacks underscores the urgency of investigating the ever-evolving tactics employed by adversaries A. As such, the study of continuously ad- vancing adversaries A becomes imperative. The proportion of users who use password managers is still low in recent years; for instance, BitWarden discovered that only 34% of people use password managers [1]. Even those who use password managers still need a user-chosen master password to protect their password manager vaults. et al. Motivation and Challenges Learning-to-rank (LTR) [23], [56], [74] plays a cru- cial role in generative retrieval [46] systems: (1) Machine translation: ranking the translations of a set of hypothe- ses. (2) Computational biology: ranking the candidate 3-D structures in protein structure prediction. (3) Recommenda- tion systems: ranking relevant news articles for users after they have read the current news article. Reward models are widely used to evaluate sequence generation in large language modelings ( e.g., RLHF [51], using given prompts to get the reward from human evaluation), to align with human preferences as much as possible. Password guessing still has a clear preference as Equation 1 as adversaries A usually attempt to guess in descending order of likelihood. Motivated by the above analysis, a natural research ques- tion arises: is it possible to propose a password guessing agent (i.e., guesser), to align the preferences of learning to rank in password guessing . To answer the question is not straightforward, and here we explain why. In ad-hoc password guessing, given an additional query information q ∈ Q (i.e., PII, and partial password) and a set of N password candidates G = {p1, p2, . . . , pN } from a password space C, a guessing model f aims to associate a relevance score f (q, pn) with each pair (q, pn) ∈ Q × C to rank the whole password set based on their relevance to q. For example, the ranking model outputs the guessing list L = [pN , pN −1, . . . , p1] if it determines that f (q, pN ) > f (q, pN −1) > · · · > f (q, p1) , (1) as adversaries A usually attempt to guess in descending order of likelihood, just as generative retrieval learning to rank. We divide the aforementioned process into three parts: • Learning to generate: generate guess candidates for different scenarios #1-#3 in Table 1 via the guesser, • Learning to rank: learn which passwords are ranking towards the top in password space C via the ranker. • Instructing to guess: with the aforementioned two ca- pabilities, the ranker can instruct the guesser to guess. More challenges emerge as the above analysis surfaces: C1: Even minor errors would result in the failure of password guesses. Passwords are extremely short texts with rich semantics and syntax. For example, if a model generates daniel1027 it would fail at guessing d@niel1027. This imposes more constraints on the exact match in Section 1.1 mentioned three tasks [36], [83] and needs more additional restrictions when generating guesses. C2: How to design rewards for password guessing task. Password guessing can be regarded as a learning-to-rank problem, which generates guesses ranking via likelihood in descending order. Fundamentally, a reward signal is an ab- straction of the task and serves as the bridge through which we convey the task objective to the agent. Designing rewards in password guessing can be a daunting task, as defining desired behaviors through reward signals can be challenging or may necessitate numerous expert demonstrations. In the learning process for generating and ranking, we need to assign a suitable reward to each state of the password, fol- lowed by the calculation of the cumulative reward collection for the entire password generation trajectory. C3: How to utilize additional information to guess users' passwords. The construction of passwords typically involves PII or commonly used strings, and adversaries A may acquire partial passwords (e.g., d****l*02*) through various means. How can a guessing model for individual users be learned from the additional available information? Wang et al. proposed solutions for traditional matching methods in Targuess-I [81] and RFGuess-PII [83]. However, there is no clear-cut solution for deep learning approaches here. The challenge lies in maximizing the success rate by leveraging additional information with a limited guesses. 1.2. Our contributions In this work, our key contributions are three-fold: • A new technical password guessing route.
